title: Telescopes
lead: A telescope gathers far more light than the eye and makes a distant object subtend a larger angle, so you can see more of its detail. Two lenses, or a mirror and a lens, form the image of a distant object. The focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece give the angular magnification, and some telescopes work with radio waves and x rays instead of light.
objectives: Outline the invention of a telescope.
Describe the working of a telescope.
summary_html:
• Simple telescopes can be made with two lenses. They are used for viewing objects at large distances and utilize the entire range of the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • The angular magnification $M$ for a telescope is given by $$M=\frac{\theta '}{\theta}=-\frac{\kfobj}{\kfeye}\text{,}$$ where $\theta$ is the angle subtended by an object viewed by the unaided eye, $\theta '$ is the angle subtended by a magnified image, and $\kfobj$ and $\kfeye$ are the focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece.
notes: Three of the module’s six problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the distance between the lenses of the telescope in the first problem for a final image very far away; the angular magnification of a small telescope with a mirror of 2.00 m radius of curvature and the angles of a sunspot and its image; and the Construct Your Own Problem item on Galileo’s telescope. The line “Unless otherwise stated, the lens-to-retina distance is 2.00 cm,” which the book prints above the module’s problems, belongs to the problems of 26.1 and is left out here. The AP item on two concave lenses is set as the book prints it, although two concave lenses cannot form a telescope; its keyed answer is (c). The AP item on a spherical mirror telescope shows the drawing for its part (a) only.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 26.23) (a) Galileo made telescopes with a convex objective and a concave eyepiece. These produce an upright image and are used in spyglasses. (b) Most simple telescopes have two convex lenses. The objective forms a case 1 image that is the object for the eyepiece. The eyepiece forms a case 2 final image that is magnified. (Figure 26.24) This arrangement of three lenses in a telescope produces an upright final image. The first two lenses are far enough apart that the second lens inverts the image of the first one more time. The third lens acts as a magnifier and keeps the image upright and in a location that is easy to view.

A two-element telescope composed of a mirror as the objective and a lens for the eyepiece is shown. This telescope forms an image in the same manner as the two-convex-lens telescope already discussed, but it does not suffer from chromatic aberrations. Such telescopes can gather more light, since larger mirrors than lenses can be constructed.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following is an advantage to using a concave mirror in the construction of a telescope? (I) The telescope can gather more light than a telescope using lenses. (II) The telescope does not suffer from chromatic aberration. (III) The telescope can provide greater magnification than a telescope using lenses.

answer.hint: Mirrors can be made much larger than lenses, a mirror reflects every color alike, and a large, relatively flat mirror has a very long focal length.

figure.alt: The image shows three shapes. At the lower left, there is an ellipse with horizontal axis. Above the ellipse is a small, tilted plane. On the right side is a vertical, curved shape (one side concave and one convex).

exercises.prompt: A spherical mirror is used to construct a telescope. (a) Using the picture below, draw two rays incident on the object mirror and continue their path through the eye lens. (b) The plane mirror is replaced with a concave lens. Using the picture below, draw the path of two incident rays. (c) Using the concave lens setup, describe the final image created by the concave lens.

answer.solution: (a) Draw two rays parallel to the axis striking the concave mirror. Each reflects toward the mirror’s focal point, but the small plane mirror intercepts the converging rays before they meet and turns them down toward the eye lens. They cross at the image, just inside the focal length of the eye lens, which sends them on to the eye. (b) With a concave lens in place of the plane mirror, the parallel rays pass beside the lens, reflect from the concave mirror toward its focal point, and meet the concave lens before they reach that point. The concave lens makes them diverge again, as the eyepiece of Galileo’s telescope does, so draw them leaving the lens to the left, less convergent than before. (c) Compare this with Galileo’s telescope, in which a diverging lens intercepts the rays before the first image forms: the rays are not turned over, so the final image is upright rather than inverted, and it is smaller than the image the mirror alone would form.

exercises.prompt: Two concave lenses, of focal lengths 500 mm and 20 mm, are used in the construction of a telescope. Given any potential arrangement, what is the largest possible magnification the telescope may have?

answer.hint: The angular magnification is the ratio of the focal lengths, with the longer one as the objective and the shorter one as the eyepiece.

exercises.prompt: If you want your microscope or telescope to project a real image onto a screen, how would you change the placement of the eyepiece relative to the objective?

answer.solution: Move the eyepiece farther from the objective. For viewing, the first image sits just inside the focal length of the eyepiece, so the eyepiece forms a large virtual image (case 2). Move the eyepiece away until the first image lies outside its focal length, and the eyepiece acts on it as a case 1 lens and forms a real image on the far side, which a screen can catch. The farther the first image is beyond the focal point, the closer and smaller the projected image becomes.

exercises.prompt: What is the angular magnification of a telescope that has a 100 cm focal length objective and a 2.50 cm focal length eyepiece?

answer.hint: Use $M = -\kfobj/\kfeye$; the sign says whether the image is inverted.

exercises.prompt: A large reflecting telescope has an objective mirror with a $10.0\ \text{m}$ radius of curvature. What angular magnification does it produce when a 3.00 cm focal length eyepiece is used?

answer.hint: The focal length of a spherical mirror is half its radius of curvature; then use $M = -\kfobj/\kfeye$ with both lengths in the same units.

exercises.prompt: A $7.5\times$ binocular produces an angular magnification of $-7.50$, acting like a telescope. (Mirrors are used to make the image upright.) If the binoculars have objective lenses with a 75.0 cm focal length, what is the focal length of the eyepiece lenses?
